opening: OSHA 1910.67 covers vehicle-mounted aerial devices such as bucket trucks; on extensible and articulating boom platforms, only trained persons may operate the lift, and anyone working from it must wear a personal fall arrest or travel restraint system attached to the boom or basket.

enforcementSummary: 1910.67(c)(2)(v) drew 457 of the 618 citations in FY2022–FY2026. It requires anyone working from an aerial lift to wear fall protection tied to the boom or basket. Next came 1910.67(c)(2)(ii), which limits operation to trained persons, with 86, then 1910.67(c)(2)(iv), which bars sitting or climbing on the basket edge, with 18. Yearly citations went from 114 in FY2022 to 130 in FY2023 and 136 in FY2024, then 135 in FY2025 and 103 in FY2026.
requirementsIntro: 1910.67 applies to vehicle-mounted aerial devices used to raise personnel to jobsites above ground: extensible boom platforms, aerial ladders, articulating boom platforms, vertical towers and combinations of these (1910.67(b)(1)). It does not cover firefighting equipment. It also does not cover the carrier vehicles, except for the rule that the vehicle must be a stable support (1910.67(b)(3)). The section has definitions in (a), general requirements in (b) and specific requirements in (c). The groups below give the main rules, and the full text has more.

requirements.heading: Which vehicles and aerial devices does 1910.67 cover?
requirements.intro: 1910.67 covers aerial devices, which it defines as vehicle-mounted devices, telescoping, articulating or both, that are used to position personnel.

items.text: An aerial device is any vehicle-mounted device, telescoping or articulating or both, that is used to position personnel.
The covered types are extensible boom platforms, aerial ladders, articulating boom platforms, vertical towers and any combination of them.
A platform is any personnel-carrying basket or bucket that forms part of an aerial device.
A vehicle is any carrier that is not manually propelled.
Firefighting equipment is outside the section.
The vehicle carrying the aerial device is outside the section, except that it must be a stable support for the aerial device.

requirements.heading: What design and modification rules apply to aerial lifts?
requirements.intro: Aerial lifts acquired from July 1, 1975 onward must be designed and built to ANSI A92.2-1969 unless the section provides otherwise, and any field modification needs written certification.

items.text: Unless 1910.67 provides otherwise, aerial lifts acquired on or after July 1, 1975 must be designed and constructed to the applicable requirements of ANSI A92.2-1969, including its appendix.

A lift acquired for use before July 1, 1975 that does not meet ANSI A92.2-1969 may not be used after July 1, 1976 unless it has been modified to conform to that standard's design and construction requirements.

A lift may be field modified for uses the manufacturer did not intend only if the manufacturer or an equivalent entity, such as a nationally recognized testing laboratory, certifies in writing that the modification conforms to ANSI A92.2-1969 and 1910.67 and that the equipment is at least as safe as it was before.
Critical hydraulic and pneumatic components, those whose failure would cause free fall or free rotation of the boom, must comply with ANSI A92.2-1969 Section 4.9 on bursting safety factor.
Noncritical hydraulic and pneumatic components must have a bursting safety factor of at least two to one.
Welding must conform, as applicable, to the American Welding Society standards listed in the paragraph: AWS B3.0-41, AWS D8.4-61, AWS D10.9-69 and AWS D2.0-69.

requirements.heading: Who may operate the lift and how must the controls work?
requirements.intro: Under 1910.67(c)(2), which covers extensible and articulating boom platforms, only trained persons may operate an aerial lift, and the lift controls must be tested each day before use.

items.text: Only trained persons may operate an aerial lift.
Lift controls must be tested each day prior to use to determine that they are in safe working condition.
Articulating and extensible boom platforms primarily designed as personnel carriers must have both platform (upper) and lower controls.
Upper controls must be in or beside the platform, within easy reach of the operator.
Lower controls must be able to override the upper controls.
Every control must be plainly marked as to its function.
Lower level controls may not be operated without permission from the employee in the lift, except in an emergency.

requirements.heading: What must workers do while in the basket?
requirements.intro: A worker in an aerial lift must wear fall protection that meets subpart I of part 1910 and must stand firmly on the basket floor, according to 1910.67(c)(2).

items.text: Wear a personal fall arrest or travel restraint system that meets subpart I, anchored to the lift's own boom or basket, when working from an aerial lift.
Do not belt off to an adjacent pole, structure or piece of equipment while working from the lift.
Stand firmly on the floor of the basket, and do not sit or climb on its edge.
Do not use planks, ladders or other devices as a work position in the basket.
Do not wear climbers while performing work from an aerial lift.
Do not exceed the boom and basket load limits specified by the manufacturer.

requirements.heading: How must the truck be set up and moved?
requirements.intro: An aerial lift truck must have its brakes set, its outriggers (when used) on pads or a solid surface and its wheels chocked on an incline, and it may not travel with the boom raised and workers aboard unless it is designed for that.

items.text: The brakes must be set.
Outriggers, when used, must be positioned on pads or a solid surface.
Wheel chocks must be installed before an aerial lift is used on an incline.

The truck may not be moved while the boom is elevated in a working position with workers in the basket, unless the equipment is specifically designed for that operation under 1910.67(b)(1) and (b)(2).

Before the lift is moved for travel, the boom or booms must be inspected to confirm they are properly cradled and the outriggers are stowed, except for equipment covered by the exception in 1910.67(c)(2)(viii).

On ladder trucks and tower trucks, aerial ladders must be secured in the lower traveling position before highway travel, using the locking device above the cab and the manually operated device at the ladder base, or other equally effective means.

requirements.heading: What electrical testing and insulation rules apply?
requirements.intro: 1910.67(c)(3) requires electrical tests to follow ANSI A92.2-1969 Section 5, and 1910.67(c)(2)(xi) bars any change to the insulated portion of a lift that might reduce its insulating value.

items.text: An insulated aerial device is one designed for work on energized lines and apparatus.
Electrical tests must be made in conformance with Section 5 of ANSI A92.2-1969.
Equivalent DC voltage tests may replace the AC voltage test, and DC tests approved by the equipment manufacturer or an equivalent entity count as equivalent.
The insulated portion of an aerial lift must not be altered in any manner that might reduce its insulating value.
For work near overhead electric lines, the section points to 1910.333(c)(3).

checklistIntro: This checklist covers equipment records, controls, truck setup, work in the basket and travel under 1910.67; use it before an aerial lift goes up and again before the truck is moved.

faq.question: Is a telescopic derrick with a personnel platform covered by 1910.67?
faq.answer: Yes. Under 1910.67(a)(4), a telescopic derrick fitted with a personnel platform attachment is treated as an extensible boom platform when it is used with that platform.

faq.question: Does a lift that cannot rotate, or one that is manually operated, still count as an aerial lift?
faq.answer: Yes. 1910.67(b)(1) says aerial equipment may be made of metal, wood, fiberglass reinforced plastic or other material, may be powered or manually operated, and is an aerial lift whether or not it can rotate about a substantially vertical axis.

faq.question: What is a vertical tower under 1910.67?
faq.answer: 1910.67(a)(9) defines a vertical tower as an aerial device designed to raise a platform along a substantially vertical axis.
